reasoning_traces.think:
The core idea of Bayesian calibration hinges on treating model outputs as noisy observations of underlying true probabilities. The hierarchical logistic model assumes that each group (e.g., sport or market) has its own deviation from a global calibration curve, modeled via random effects. This allows for shrinkage towards global parameters, stabilizing estimates in low-data regimes. The use of Empirical Bayes (EB) τ provides data-driven control over this shrinkage, balancing between group-specific adaptability and global consistency. In contrast, Platt scaling applies a smooth transformation to raw logits using Bayesian priors on linear coefficients, offering a continuous mapping but assuming the raw scores approximate true probabilities. Both methods are evaluated via offline bake-offs against frequentist baselines such as Brier, ECE, and Murphy reliability, ensuring that any adjustment to production systems requires rigorous validation before deployment. The key insight is that Bayesian calibration does not replace frequentist eligibility checks but enhances them with principled uncertainty quantification.
